extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, appellate counsel, patent litigators, PTO/PTAB practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Appellate review of a PTAB inter partes review decision addressing obviousness (including secondary considerations such as unexpected results) and the written-description requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112. The page records parties' arguments over whether the Board properly considered objective indicia and a companion decision finding lack of written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof in IPR: preponderant evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Mylan failed to demonstrate by preponderant evidence that the challenged claims were unpatentable as obvious over a combination of prior-art references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTAB's determination of unpatentability in an inter partes review is evaluated under the preponderance‑of‑the‑evidence standard; a challenger must show that invalidity is more likely than not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness over combinations of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the challenged claims are unpatentable as obvious over a combination of prior‑art references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness analysis requires examining whether a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine the prior art to arrive at the claimed invention; the Board found Mylan did not meet its burden to show obviousness over the cited references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia (secondary considerations) such as unexpected results, commercial success, long‑felt need, and failure of others may be considered in the nonobviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mylan argued the Board erred in its analysis of secondary considerations and that limiting its determination to unexpected results (while ignoring disputes over the 'other three objective indicia') violated the APA. Biogen argued there is no requirement that the Board consider all objective indicia before making a nonobviousness determination. The page records this dispute but does not resolve it on the merits because of a dispositive written‑description holding in a companion case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results as a persuasive secondary consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the claimed invention produced unexpected results may overcome a prima facie obviousness showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board determined that Biogen presented sufficient evidence of unexpected results to overcome Mylan's obviousness challenge (see PTAB findings cited on the page). The court's summary reports this as the Board's basis for upholding patentability on obviousness grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112; lack of adequate written description can render a patent invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The companion Federal Circuit decision held the '514 patent invalid for lack of written description under § 112; that holding is dispositive of the PTAB's patentability determination in this appeal, so the court did not reach the merits of the parties' remaining arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) procedural challenge to PTAB decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may contend the PTAB's decision violated the APA by failing to address or by improperly limiting consideration of disputed issues (e.g., considering only one secondary consideration while ignoring others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mylan argued the Board violated the APA by issuing a determination limited only to unexpected results and ignoring the parties' dispute over other objective indicia; Biogen responded that there is no requirement to consider all objective indicia. The court here did not address the APA issue because of the intervening written‑description disposition.
